title: [Remote Sensing] A Few-Shot Method Based on Spatial-Frequency Dual-Domain Feature Enhancement and Hypersphere Mapping Constraint for SAR Ship Recognition
abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) can acquire maritime imagery independently of daylight and under diverse weather conditions, which makes it well suited to persistent ship monitoring and maritime awareness. Nevertheless, recognizing SAR ships from only a few labeled examples remains difficult for several reasons. First, sea clutter and speckle noise may weaken ship-related structural and scattering-response information. Second, features from different categories may become difficult to separate because between-class differences are small while within-class variations remain substantial. Third, when each category contains only a few support examples, an abnormal or noisy sample can noticeably distort the estimated prototype. To address these issues, a few-shot SAR ship recognition method based on spatial-frequency dual-domain feature enhancement and hypersphere mapping constraint (SFHMC) is proposed. First, the spatial-frequency feature enhancement and extraction module (SFEE) combines the Haar discrete wavelet transform with multi-scale spatial modeling. It enhances structural, textural, and scattering-response features under complex backgrounds. Second, the hypersphere mapping constraint module (HMCM) normalizes support and query embeddings onto a unit hypersphere. By removing differences in feature magnitude, this mapping makes similarity estimation depend mainly on feature direction and produces a more structured class distribution. Third, the sample-weighted prototype generation module (SWPGM) adaptively adjusts the contribution of each support sample according to its consistency with the initial class prototype. This reduces prototype bias caused by noisy or atypical samples. The three modules jointly optimize feature representation, metric discrimination, and prototype calibration. Experiments are conducted on FUSAR-Ship and OpenSARShip, with additional validation on MSTAR under 3-way 1-shot and 3-way 5-shot settings. Compared with MBEN-BC, SFHMC improves classification accuracy by 1.41 and 1.96 percentage points on FUSAR-Ship, 2.68 and 4.46 percentage points on OpenSARShip, and 6.40 and 0.48 percentage points on MSTAR, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of SFHMC for few-shot SAR target recognition under limited data and complex imaging conditions.

title: [Remote Sensing] Echo-Driven Doppler Parameter Estimation for High-Resolution Squinted Spaceborne Sliding Spotlight SAR
abstract: High-resolution squinted spaceborne sliding spotlight synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging requires accurate Doppler parameters. In conventional SAR processing, Doppler parameters are generally derived from prior ancillary information or estimated from the received echoes. However, Doppler parameters derived from prior information are sensitive to ancillary-measurement errors, while existing echo-based methods remain insufficient for ambiguity-resolved Doppler-centroid estimation and Doppler frequency modulation (FM)-rate refinement in high-resolution squinted sliding spotlight SAR. To reduce the reliance on prior ancillary information for Doppler-parameter determination, this paper proposes an echo-driven Doppler-parameter estimation (ED-DPE) method. The proposed method first estimates the baseband Doppler centroid using adjacent-echo cross-correlation and then resolves the Doppler ambiguity number based on the range-migration slope, thereby obtaining the absolute Doppler centroid fd. The estimated absolute Doppler centroid is subsequently used as a physical constraint on an attitude-equivalent observation geometry, which is refined through contrast-based full-aperture image formation to obtain the Doppler FM rate fr and the imaging parameters. Point-target simulations and real spaceborne SAR experiments demonstrate that the proposed ED-DPE method supports accurate focusing of 0.25-m-resolution squinted sliding spotlight SAR.

title: [Remote Sensing] Mapping Seasonal and Persistent Surface-Current Regimes Using Long-Term HF Radar Observations and Physics-Guided Clustering
abstract: Long-term high-frequency radar (HFR) observations provide a unique opportunity to examine how coastal surface currents organise into recurrent current-field configurations. This study uses the 2013–2024 HFR-Lisbon surface-current record to identify sub-inertial regimes in the Lisbon coastal region, a dynamically complex sector of the western Iberian margin. Hourly HFR currents were quality controlled, filtered with a centred 33 h rolling mean and restricted to a sub-inertial analysis domain defined from long-term coverage and residual semidiurnal-energy criteria. A physics-guided K-means clustering approach was then applied to seven physically interpretable descriptors of current intensity, directional coherence, spatial contrast, temporal change and bathymetry-based current-speed distribution. Four recurrent regimes were identified: a low-energy regime, a shelf-intensified regime, a moderate slope/offshore regime and an energetic offshore-intensified regime. The regimes show coherent spatial structures, marked seasonal organisation, persistence over several days and preferential temporal pathways. ERA5 winds, analysed a posteriori, show the strongest contrast between the low-energy regime, associated primarily with weaker-than-average winds, and the energetic offshore-intensified regime, associated with stronger and more northerly wind conditions. The results demonstrate the value of long-term HFR observations and physics-guided clustering for identifying and interpreting recurrent coastal surface-current configurations.

title: [Remote Sensing] Water Quality Variation Among Optical Water Types Along the Guangdong Coast: Additional Within-Class Information from Membership Structure
abstract: Coastal waters exhibit pronounced spatial and temporal variability in optical properties and water quality, which cannot be fully characterized by observations from discrete monitoring stations. Satellite Optical Water Type (OWT) classification provides spatially continuous information on optical conditions. However, comparisons with water quality observations have generally relied on the assigned OWT, and it remains unclear whether membership provides additional information within the same class. This study examined the relationships of assigned OWTs and membership with monthly water quality conditions in Guangdong coastal waters. Sentinel-3 OLCI observations acquired from 2017 to 2024 were matched with station observations of dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN), dissolved inorganic phosphorus (DIP), chemical oxygen demand (COD), dissolved oxygen (DO), and eutrophication classes. The analysis first compared water quality among assigned OWTs and then evaluated the secondary OWT and membership values within OWT 4a, the class with the largest sample size. Assigned OWTs distinguished broad differences in DIN, DIP, COD, and eutrophication classes, whereas DO did not differ significantly among OWTs. Within OWT 4a, the class associated with the second highest membership separated records with different nutrient, COD, and eutrophication conditions. Continuous membership values provided further information, but their relationships with water quality depended on the secondary OWT and were most consistent for DIN. OWT occurrence and station eutrophication patterns showed partial spatial correspondence, particularly around the Pearl River Estuary and Huangmao Bay. These findings show that assigned OWTs identify broad water quality differences, while secondary OWTs and membership values distinguish additional variation within OWT 4a. The mapped optical patterns provide complementary spatial context for interpreting station-based water quality observations.

title: [Forests] Soil C:N:P Stoichiometric Differences Between Farmland and Shelterbelts and Their Associations with Soil Physicochemical Properties in the Yellow River Floodplain
abstract: Shelterbelts are an important component of ecological restoration in the Yellow River Floodplain, but their associations with soil carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) stoichiometry remain incompletely understood. We compared farmland and shelterbelt soils at two depths (0–20 and 20–40 cm) and examined how nutrient indicators were associated with soil physicochemical properties. In the 0–20 cm layer, C/N, C/P, and N/P ratios were significantly higher in shelterbelt than in farmland, whereas total P and inorganic N contents were higher in farmland. Soil organic carbon and total N generally decreased with depth under both land uses. Factorial analysis identified significant land use × soil depth interactions for total P and all three stoichiometric ratios, indicating that their depth-related changes differed between farmland and shelterbelt. Correlation and random forest analyses showed that soil water content, bulk density, particle-size characteristics, and pH were associated with nutrient indicators, with their relative importance varying by land use and depth. These findings reveal land-use- and depth-dependent differences in soil C:N:P stoichiometry and identify soil properties relevant to monitoring soil quality during shelterbelt management in the Yellow River Floodplain.

title: [Remote Sensing] Effect of Sun Glints from Ice Clouds on MODIS Data Products
abstract: This paper examines the way sun glints from horizontally oriented ice crystals that occur in clouds impact atmospheric data products provided by the Moderate-Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS). For this, the paper presents a statistical analysis of two years of MODIS data from all tropical land regions. The results indicate only weak glint effects on cloud amount and height, as these values are obtained using mainly observations of (inherently glint-free) thermal infrared radiation. In contrast, glints are found to cause a roughly 10% increase in mean retrieved cloud optical thickness, and 10% decreases in mean particle size and in the prevalence of ice cloud phase. Moreover, glints from undetected ice clouds are found to cause roughly 5% increases in mean aerosol optical depth and coarse mode fraction, and positive and negative biases comparable to the magnitude of the seasonal cycle in total column ozone and precipitable water vapor amounts, respectively. Given the modest size of glints, the effects are most important to consider in studies that use data from a limited range of viewing zenith angles (e.g., around nadir). The results are relevant to MODIS and to other satellite imagers that use similar retrieval algorithms, and thus likely experience similar glint effects.

In contrast, glints are found to cause a roughly 10% increase in mean retrieved cloud optical thickness, and 10% decreases in mean particle size and in the prevalence of ice cloud phase. Moreover, glints from undetected ice clouds are found to cause roughly 5% increases in mean aerosol optical depth and coarse mode fraction, and positive and negative biases comparable to the magnitude of the seasonal cycle in total column ozone and precipitable water vapor amounts, respectively. Given the modest size of glints, the effects are most important to consider in studies that use data from a limited range of viewing zenith angles (e.g., around nadir). The results are relevant to MODIS and to other satellite imagers that use similar retrieval algorithms, and thus likely experience similar glint effects.

title: [Forests] Developmental Stage Changes in Populus euphratica Alter the Rhizosphere Fungal Community Structure in Arid Environments
abstract: In arid environments, rhizosphere microbial communities change with plant developmental stages. This partly reflects the coordinated adaptation of plant-microbe interactions under stress. Our study explored the effects of Populus euphratica at different developmental stages on rhizosphere fungal communities under drought conditions. Illumina NovaSeq sequencing was performed to characterize fungal community structures across stands at different developmental stages. Significant differences in fungal α-diversity were detected among age groups. The mature developmental stage exhibited the highest species richness and diversity indices (Chao1 = 507.33, Shannon = 6.64), along with the largest proportion of unique amplicon sequence variants (ASVs, 29.04%). In contrast, the near-mature developmental stage showed the lowest values for these indicators (Chao1 = 166.62, Shannon = 4.24, unique ASVs = 6.29%). Ascomycota dominated across all developmental stages (52.36%–88.41%), whereas Basidiomycota was more abundant in over-mature and declining developmental stages (3.96%, 3.35%). Predicted functional types mainly included saprotroph, pathotroph-saprotroph and pathotroph-saprotroph-symbiotroph. The near-mature forest had the lowest co-occurrence network complexity (average degree = 9.18, total edge number = 234). The network complexity exhibited a non-monotonic pattern, characterized by a sharp decline at the near-mature developmental stage, followed by stabilization in the mature, over-mature and declining developmental stages. Fungal communities in all developmental stages exhibited deterministic assembly patterns. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) indicated that forest age correlated with soil nutrient differences. These soil nutrient differences, in turn, correlated with variations in fungal community structure. Overall, P. euphratica developmental stage was closely related to the rhizosphere microenvironment and fungal community structure. Using a space-for-time substitution approach, our study elucidated the variation patterns of rhizosphere fungal communities of P. euphratica along the forest developmental stages gradient in arid areas. Nevertheless, the mechanisms underlying temporal succession need to be further validated by long-term permanent monitoring.

title: [Forests] Forest Type and Soil Properties Shape Fungal Communities and Astraeus Distribution Across Forest Ecosystems
abstract: Astraeus is an ectomycorrhizal fungus that forms symbiotic associations with trees of the families Dipterocarpaceae and Pinaceae and is typically distributed in dry dipterocarp forests in northern and northeastern Thailand. However, knowledge of the composition and diversity of fungal communities in areas where Astraeus occurs remains limited. Therefore, this study investigated soil fungal community composition and diversity associated with Astraeus in five Thai forest types and identified key environmental drivers using NGS amplicon sequencing targeting the ITS1 region of the rRNA gene. These forests harbored abundant fungal communities, particularly ectomycorrhizal fungi. Forests where Astraeus was detected (DDF and PDDF) exhibited distinct fungal community composition and diversity compared with those without Astraeus (dry evergreen forest (DEF), lower montane pine–oak forest (LMPF), and tropical evergreen rain forest (TEF)). Soil properties, particularly clay content, differed significantly between Astraeus-detected and Astraeus-not-detected soils; although there was a tendency toward higher sand content in Astraeus-detected soils, this was not statistically significant. Overall, the occurrence of Astraeus is primarily driven by forest type and soil properties, highlighting its role in forest fungal diversity.

title: [Forests] Red, White, and Yellow Tubes Enhance PAR Reflectance and Seedling Quality of Corymbia citriodora (Hook.) K.D.Hill & L.A.S.Johnson in Combination with a Bioinoculant Based on Chlorella vulgaris Beijerinck
authors: Fernanda Pacheco de Almeida Prado Bortolheiro
abstract: Eucalypt cultivation (Eucalyptus and Corymbia spp.) in Brazil is extensive, primarily due to its rapid growth, adaptability, high yield potential, and suitability for different production chains. Consequently, attention must be given to the quality and health of its propagation materials since high-quality seedlings show greater field survival and growth performance. Therefore, the present study aimed to evaluate the performance of Corymbia citriodora (Hook.) K.D.Hill & L.A.S.Johnson, seedlings cultivated in tube trays of different colors, in order to assess how colour-driven differences in light reflectance affect seedling growth and physiology, and treated with a microalga-based bioinoculant (Chlorella vulgaris Beijerinck). The experiment was conducted at the Mato Grosso do Sul State University, Cassilândia Campus. The trial followed a completely randomized design in a 5 × 2 factorial scheme (four tray/tube colors plus control × bioinoculant application plus control), with four independent trays (replications) per combination. The bright colors used were white, red, blue, and yellow in 96-cell trays. Applications were performed at 60 and 90 days after sowing (DAS). At 97 DAS, the number of leaves, seedling height and shoot diameter, along with shoot, root, and total dry masses, were evaluated. Data were analyzed using the Sisvar software, and seedling quality was assessed by the Dickson Quality Index. The use of colored trays and tubes represents a promising technique for producing C. citriodora seedlings, particularly those with higher light reflectance. Cultivation in white or red trays and applying a Chlorella vulgaris-based bioinoculant promotes high-quality C. citriodora seedlings. Using trays with white, yellow, and red tubes enhances the physiological potential of C. citriodora seedlings. The bioinoculant significantly increased chlorophyll b content in seedlings grown in blue, red, and control trays.

title: [Forests] Electrocution of Japanese Knotweed (Reynoutria japonica Houtt.) Rhizome Sprouts Under Controlled Conditions: Implications for Forest Management
abstract: Invasive weeds threaten forest ecosystem sustainability worldwide, underscoring the need for non-chemical management strategies. To address this challenge, the present study investigated the short-term morphological response and survival of the Japanese knotweed (Reynoutria japonica Houtt.) rhizome sprouts subjected to 60-s electrocution at 0–180 V in 20-V increments. The one-way ANOVA showed no significant effect on sprout diameter (p > 0.05), whereas sprout length varied significantly (p < 0.05; η2 = 0.540), with Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test revealing that mean sprout length ranged from 20.9 ± 2.1 cm to 42.6 ± 4.6 cm for sprouts subjected to 60 V and 180 V, respectively. In contrast, the Mantel–Cox trend test indicated a significant decline in sprout survival time with increasing voltage (χ2(1) = 29.028; p < 0.001), as reflected by the Kaplan–Meier analysis. Furthermore, the Cox proportional hazards model showed a 2.60% increase in mortality hazard per 1-V increase (HR = 1.026; p < 0.001). These results indicate that electrocution treatments of ≥100 V induce rapid sprout mortality, with complete mortality observed by day 3 at 100 and 180 V and by day 4 at 120–160 V, a response descriptively referred to as the “flash-kill” effect, and highlight survival analysis as a more informative indicator for evaluating R. japonica electrocution efficacy. Nevertheless, even though short-term sprout mortality is not a definitive measure of control, a long-term evaluation must account for rhizome reserve depletion, bud number and viability, as well as sprout reemergence under forest-oriented, field-scale studies.
